newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan leader blames China for stalled relations.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan leader blames China for stalled relations.

text.p: Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui on Wednesday blamed rival Beijing for its attempts to isolate the island diplomatically, saying such behaviour was "detrimental" to national reunification.
Lee, in a written statement for the island's October 10th National Day, urged China to step up dialogue and communication and actively safeguard the stability of the Taiwan Straits.

"The existence and development of the Republic of China on Taiwan is a fact witnessed by the whole world; it is also an undeniable fact that Taiwan and the Chinese mainland are ruled by two distinct governments," Lee said in the speech.
Taiwan is ruled by the Republic of China government that lost a civil war to the Chinese communists in 1949 and went into exile on the island.
Beijing, which views Taiwan as a rebel-held province, vehemently opposes Taipei's effort to break its international isolation and threatens to retake the island by force if it opts for independence.
"Regrettably, the Chinese communist authorities ignore the right of our 21.3 million people to exist, and persistently deny our warm devotion to world civilisation," the president said.
"They constantly utilise power politics to undermine our international status and hinder our attempt to raise our international profile."
Ties between Beijing and Taipei plunged after the private, but high-profile, visit by President Lee to the United States in June 1995.
A furious Beijing then said the visit showed that Lee wanted Taiwan's independence and not reunification with the mainland.

China angerly suspended semi-official talks with Taipei and rattled Taiwan with war games and missile tests off the island before its first direct presidential elections in March, which Lee won by a landslide.

"This sort of behaviour swims against the world tide of democracy and freedom...harms feelings between the people on each side of the Taiwan Straits, and is detrimental to national reunificaiton," Lee said.
Lee reiterated his willingness to embark upon a "journey of peace" to China and to meet with top leadership in Beijing for direct exchange of views.

"Nonetheless, the Chinese communist authorities remain unable to set aside their prejudices and face the fact that both sides co-exist, thus preventing cross-Straits relations from moving ahead," he said.

Beijing's top negotiator with Taipei on Tuesday said the reunification of China and Taiwan would become a more glaring issue after the nearby Portuguese enclave of Macau reverts to Chinese rule in 1999.

"The Taiwan problem will stand out in front of us after Hong Kong's return in 1997 and Macau's return in 1999," Tang Shubei, vice-chairman of the Association for Relations Across the Taiwan Straits, said in Beijing.
Tang said time and patience were needed for China and Taiwan to reunify, but declined to spell out a timetable.

Last week, China accused Taiwan of standing in the way of reunification by creating obstacles to economic and trade cooperation, saying the island was "squashing its own feet with a rock" by refusing to end the direct trade ban.
